My favorite part about writing is that first spark of an idea. It can happen at any time, for any reason. The idea for the Opalite music video crash landed into my imagination when I was doing promo for The Life of a Showgirl. I was a guest on one of my favorite shows, @TheGrahamNortonShowOfficial. For those of you who aren’t familiar, it’s a UK late night show where Graham Norton (the insanely charismatic and lovable host) invites a random group of actors, entertainers, musicians, etc to be on his show and we all sit there and chat like it’s a dinner party. They even serve wine. Anyway. I remember thinking I got ridiculously lucky with the group I was paired with. Cillian Murphy, Domhnall Gleeson, Greta Lee, @JodieSmith, and @LewisCapaldi. All people whose work I’ve admired from afar. When we were all talking during the broadcast, Domhnall made a light hearted joke about wanting to be in one of my music videos. He’s Irish! He was joking! Except that in that moment during the interview, I was instantly struck with an *idea*. And so a week later he received an email script I’d written for the Opalite video, where he was playing the starring role. I had this thought that it would be wild if all of our fellow guests on the Graham Norton show that night, including Graham himself, could be a part of it too. Like a school group project but for adults and it isn’t mandatory. To my delight, everyone from the show made the effort to time travel back to the 90’s with us and help with this video. You might even recognize some friendly faces from The Eras Tour. I got to work with one of my favorite people in the world, @rpstam, again! I had more fun than I ever imagined - Made new friends, metaphors, and fashion choices. It was an absolute thrill to create this story and these characters. Shot on film. The Opalite video is out now on Spotify & Apple Music.

And, baby, that’s show business for you. New album The Life of a Showgirl. Out October 3 ❤️‍🔥

(5) Additional Strong Defenses
- **Transformative use / fair use** (17 U.S.C. § 107) — Even if some similarity existed, "Flowers" is highly transformative: it comments on/critiques the original's regret by turning it into self-reliance. *Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc.* (510 U.S. 569, 1994) protects parodies/responses. The market effect favors Cyrus—the publicity actually boosted streams of the Mars song.
- Precedent from similar weak claims — Ed Sheeran ("Thinking Out Loud" vs. Marvin Gaye), Katy Perry ("Dark Horse"), Robin Thicke ("Blurred Lines") cases show courts reject suits over common elements or vague similarities.
 Conclusion: Cyrus Is Legally Correct and Likely to Prevail
This is not a strong infringement case—it's a speculative suit by a rights investor hoping to extract a settlement from a blockbuster hit (over 1 billion streams, multiple Grammys). The similarities are superficial and confined to unprotectable ideas/tropes. Under Ninth Circuit law, substantial similarity fails both objectively and subjectively. The February 2026 summary judgment motion is well-grounded and positions Cyrus for dismissal without trial.
If the judge grants it (very plausible given the weaknesses exposed), the case ends decisively in her favor. Even if it proceeds, expert evidence and jury would likely find no infringement. U.S. law encourages creativity and response songs without monopolizing basic emotional/language tools in music. Cyrus has total legal right here—this is inspiration and cultural dialogue, not theft.

(4) Key Unprotectable Elements (Why No Infringement)
- **Chord progressions and harmonic structures** → The claimed similarities (e.g., variations on i–iv–VII–III or common pop loops like Am–Dm–G–C) are stock elements used in thousands of songs. Ninth Circuit precedent in *Skidmore v. Led Zeppelin* (952 F.3d 1051, 2020) ("Stairway to Heaven" case) held that common chord progressions and descending bass lines are not protectable due to lack of originality.
- **Lyrical tropes** → Themes of regret in relationships, buying flowers as apology, dancing/holding hands/talking—these are **scènes à faire** ("scenes that must be done") in breakup ballads. No one can monopolize them (*Mattel, Inc. v. MGA Entm't, Inc.*, 616 F.3d 904 (9th Cir. 2010)). Cyrus flips them into empowerment ("I can buy myself flowers"), creating contrast, not copying.
- **Melodic fragments** → Any short pitch sequences or bass lines are generic or too brief to be protectable. Forensic musicology analyses (cited in defenses) show clear differences in melody contour, rhythm, phrasing, and overall structure.
- **Overall dissimilarity** → Different BPM (~73 vs. ~118), genres (piano ballad vs. disco-influenced pop), vocal delivery, production, and message. An ordinary reasonable listener hears two distinct songs. ...

(3) Deep Legal Analysis: Why Miley Cyrus Has a Strong (Likely Winning) Position Under U.S. Copyright Law
U.S. copyright law (Copyright Act of 1976, 17 U.S.C. §§ 101 et seq.) protects **original expression**, not ideas, facts, or common elements (17 U.S.C. § 102(b)). To win, Tempo must prove:
1. Ownership of a valid copyright → Yes, Tempo has partial ownership.
2. Access by Cyrus → Undisputed (massive hit song).
3. **Substantial similarity** between protectable elements → This is where the case collapses for Tempo.
Courts use a two-part test (Ninth Circuit: extrinsic/intrinsic, from cases like *Sid & Marty Krofft Television Prods., Inc. v. McDonald's Corp.*, 562 F.2d 1157 (9th Cir. 1977)):
- **Extrinsic (objective)**: Dissection by experts—do similarities exist in protectable expression?
- **Intrinsic (subjective)**: Would an ordinary listener think one was copied from the other? ...

(2) - **Most recent development (February 24, 2026)**: Cyrus's legal team filed a **motion for summary judgment** (under Fed. R. Civ. P. 56), asking the court to dismiss the case without a full trial. Their core arguments:
 - No **substantial similarity** exists in the protectable elements of the two songs.
 - Any similarities involve **unprotectable ideas** or **commonplace tropes** in breakup songs (e.g., references to buying flowers, holding hands, dancing, talking for hours).
 - Lyrics like "I should have bought you flowers" (Mars) vs. "I can buy myself flowers" (Cyrus) are not owned by anyone—"No one owns these words."
 - The songs are "very different" overall: different tempos, keys, arrangements, vocal styles, and themes (regret and pleading in Mars vs. self-empowerment and independence in Cyrus).
 - "Flowers" is a classic **"answer song"** or response track—a longstanding, protected form of musical dialogue—not an unauthorized derivative work. ...
This motion is pending; no ruling has been issued yet (as of February 25, 2026). If granted, it would end the case in Cyrus's favor without a jury trial. If denied, the matter could proceed toward discovery, expert testimony (e.g., musicologists), and potentially trial. ...

(1) The lawsuit against Miley Cyrus regarding her 2023 hit **"Flowers"** and alleged copyright infringement of Bruno Mars' 2013 song **"When I Was Your Man"** remains ongoing as of February 25, 2026, in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California (case no. 2:24-cv-07910). The plaintiff is **Tempo Music Investments, LLC**, a music rights investment firm that acquired a partial co-ownership interest in "When I Was Your Man" from co-writer Philip Lawrence around 2020. Bruno Mars himself is not a plaintiff, and the case is driven by this financial entity rather than the original creators.
 Current Status (as of late February 2026)
- The case was filed in September 2024.
- In March 2025, Judge Dean D. Pregerson denied Cyrus and her co-defendants' (including co-writers Gregory Hein and Michael Pollack, plus publishers like Sony) initial motion to dismiss based on **lack of standing** by Tempo. The court ruled that a co-owner (or assignee like Tempo) can sue for infringement without joining other co-owners or obtaining their consent, consistent with 17 U.S.C. § 501(b) and Ninth Circuit precedent. This reinforced that partial rights holders retain enforcement power, which benefits the market for catalog sales.
- In November/December 2024, Cyrus filed another motion challenging standing on similar grounds, but it did not succeed in ending the case early. ...
